The scar anchor is adenoviral-EKC-specific (subepithelial infiltrates); ordinary bacterial and allergic conjunctivitis rarely scar the cornea, so the edge must not be read as applying to all conjunctivitis - keep the adenoviral anchor explicit when reviewing.
governanceNotes: Authored conservatively at ASSOCIATION_ONLY strength: the subepithelial-infiltrate pathway is documented for adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis specifically, while the catalog conjunctivitis identity spans viral, bacterial, and allergic etiologies that differ sharply in corneal behavior; no cohort reports scarring incidence across the full conjunctivitis population.

Reversibility guard recorded: the adenoviral literature describes subepithelial infiltrates as difficult-to-treat but also frequently resolving (immune deposits on Bowman layer rather than true stromal scarring), so persistence to permanent opacity must be individually documented; steroid-use complication risk noted in the source literature.

nexusClaim.associationBasis: The adenoviral-keratoconjunctivitis review records that viral protein remnants on Bowman layer provoke an immune reaction forming subepithelial infiltrates, described as the major sequelae and difficult to treat (Renard 2010); the update review confirms keratitis nummularis as the corneal manifestation of adenoviral infection (Gonzalez-Lopez 2013); the mechanism study resolves the pathway - HMGB1 secreted by infected corneal epithelial cells induces leukocytic infiltrates directly and via stimulated stromal cells, explaining subepithelial infiltrate formation in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (Saha 2025).
nexusClaim.causationStatus: Neither causation nor aggravation is established at the mapping level: the scar pathway is documented for adenoviral EKC specifically rather than conjunctivitis broadly, subepithelial infiltrates often resolve rather than persisting as permanent scarring, no cohort reports permanent-opacity incidence after conjunctivitis, and unrelated corneal disease produces identical scarring - so no directional claim is made here.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: An immune-mediated corneal-involvement pathway is documented for adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis: viral protein retention on Bowman layer triggers an immune reaction forming subepithelial infiltrates, with the HMGB1-alarmin mechanism now experimentally resolved; whether infiltrates persist as permanent opacity varies individually. The pathway is adenovirus-specific, so no directional claim is made at the conjunctivitis level.

evidentiaryProfile.conservativeRationale: This relationship is supported as an association only. Corneal subepithelial infiltrates are a recognized adenoviral-EKC sequelae; individual determination requires documentation of the adenoviral episode with chronology, corneal findings localizing the opacity, exclusion of other corneal disease, and review by a qualified medical professional.
evidentiaryProfile.evidenceGaps: documentation of the conjunctivitis episode(s) with etiology where available (adenoviral/EKC, bacterial, other) and chronology; corneal examination findings localizing the scarring (subepithelial infiltrates, stromal opacity) with laterality; exclusion of prior trauma, herpetic keratitis, contact-lens pathology, and degenerations; treatment history including topical-steroid use; a medical professional's opinion connecting the documented findings in this individual case
alternativeEtiologiesToRuleOut: Herpes simplex keratitis scarring (misremembered as conjunctivitis)
Trauma, corneal abrasion, or contact-lens-related scarring
Topical-steroid or medication toxicity effects during treatment
Bacterial or allergic conjunctivitis without corneal involvement (the majority)

suggestions.rationale: Authored conservatively at association-only strength: the subepithelial-infiltrate pathway is well documented for adenoviral EKC with the mechanism experimentally resolved, but the edge records the association without a causal claim because infiltrates often resolve and the conjunctivitis identity spans etiologies that rarely scar.
